title: Willow dog basket (small)
subtitle: Basketry: an oval willow basket with a low front wall, sized for a small to medium dog
excerpt: A small willow dog basket: oval base, low sloped front wall, high back and sides. Made in brown buff willow with a four-rod wale structure and a rope border. The low front allows easy entry; the high sides give the dog a sense of enclosure. Sized for a Whippet or Spaniel.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the oval base construction; Twining, Basketwork for Beginners (1920) for the rope border and sloped front technique.

glossaryTerms.definition: The base framework of a willow basket, made by threading rods through a central bundle to form a cross or oval structure.
A weaving pattern using multiple rods that chase each other around the basket, creating a strong structural row.
A three-rod twisted border where stakes are paired and twisted together as they are woven in, producing a plaited top edge.
Willow boiled to fix a tan colour and stripped of bark. The standard material for traditional English willow baskets.
The first rows of waling worked after staking up, which bend the side stakes upright and lock them in place.

content.text: A willow dog basket is an oval bread basket at larger scale with one change: the front wall is low so the dog can step in, while the back and side walls are tall. The structure is an oval
sides, but the front stakes are shorter and their border is worked first. Sized for a dog of 8, 12 kg (a Whippet or medium Spaniel).

: base sticks in 75 cm and 60 cm lengths, 20 side stakes at 120 cm (for the back and sides), 8 short side stakes at 65 cm (for the front), about 100 weavers in mixed lengths. Soak overnight and rest wrapped in a damp cloth for 30 minutes before starting.
Secateurs for cutting rods to length.
Side cutters for trimming ends flush.

Build an oval slath 60 cm by 40 cm using the 75 cm and 60 cm base sticks, following the same construction as the oval bread basket. The base is larger here, allow more base sticks (10 long, 8 short) for a solid foundation that can take the weight and movement of a dog. Weave the base in pairing until all sticks are covered and the base is firm.

Insert the 20 long stakes at regular intervals around the back and sides of the base. Insert the 8 shorter stakes at the front, the low front section covers about one-third of the oval. The short stakes will be worked to 25 cm high; the long stakes to 45 cm. Lock all stakes with three rounds of four-rod
wale, working all the way around to lock both long and short stakes uniformly.

Work the body in randing, going all the way around including the front section, until the front stakes are within 3 cm of their full height. At this point, the front stakes need to be brought to their border while the back and side stakes continue weaving to their full height. Work the front
at 25 cm height on the front stakes only. Then continue randing the back and sides until they reach 45 cm, and complete the rope border on all remaining stakes.

A rope border pairs adjacent stakes, twists them together, and weaves them into the neighbouring stakes to lock. Work consistently in one direction. The paired twist produces a plaited appearance that is stronger than a trac border for a basket under regular animal use. Trim all ends flush on completion.
Dry for 48 hours minimum before lining and use. Line with a flat cushion or folded blanket; the cushion can be removed for washing. No finish needed on the basket itself.

attrs.symptom: The front and back borders are at different heights when viewed from the side
attrs.cause: The front stakes were not measured correctly before the split border work began
attrs.fix: Measure the short stakes against the long stakes before staking up, and mark the height difference on each short stake with a pencil before inserting. The height difference is achieved by using shorter stakes, not by stopping the weaving at a different point.
